3. MATERIAL AND METHODS
This section outlines the research framework, sampling techniques and data analysis procedures. A descriptive research design with a quantitative focus was selected as optimal for examining the relationship between employee training, motivation, and customer engagement. This approach enabled orderly data collection and analysis, which was aligned with the study objectives. Employing a quantitative method and multiple regression analysis is considered appropriate for the research goals because it enhances the simplicity, generalizability, clarity, and statistical reliability. The analysis utilized frequencies, tables, percentages, and regression analyses to address the research question: "What effect do employee training and motivation have on customer engagement among small and medium enterprises in Mogadishu, Somalia?" Structured questionnaires were developed based on a comprehensive literature review, employing Likert scales (2= Agree,1 = Disagree) via the Kobo Toolbox to collect data from employees of small and medium-sized organizations. This platform ensures efficiency, reduces manual errors, and facilitates smooth data cleaning and export to statistical software programs. Data collection will be conducted from November 2024 to January 2025. The questionnaires were personally distributed with the assistance of leaders, managers and supervisors to gather data from staff working in small and medium sized enterprises in Mogadishu and Somalia. The researchers ensured that the distribution of the questionnaires did not interfere with the respondents' official work schedules and obtained special permission from the company leaders. The data were analyzed after cleaning and verifying the questionnaires’ completeness. The researchers utilized a simple random sampling technique, a type of probability sampling, to ensure that each individual had an equal chance of being selected, thereby accurately representing the target population (Tabiu, 2017). This method aligns with the objective of obtaining representative samples while maintaining methodological rigor. The validity of the findings was enhanced by ensuring that each participant had an equal probability of being selected. The researchers identified 301 respondents and distributed 172 questionnaires to employees of small- and medium-sized enterprises in Mogadishu, Somalia. The participants were staff members of small- and medium-sized enterprises, excluding non-staff members and those employed in non-business organizations. Slovin’s formula was employed to determine the sample size with a maximum allowable error of 5%, where n= 31/1+301 (0.05)2=172, where n represents the sample size, N is the population, and a is the acceptable error. This formula was selected because it allows sampling of the population with the desired precision. The sample size ensured representativeness with a 95% confidence level, providing a reliable estimate of population characteristics consistent with the research's quantitative objectives.  To ensure the accuracy of the data, the questionnaires were examined by specialists with an understanding of staff training, motivation, and customer engagement among SME's in the Banadir region of Mogadishu, Somalia, ensuring that they included all important parts of the study. This means that it communicates accurate data that are compatible with respondents’ information and expectations. The quantity of built-in measurement errors determines the validity of the research instrument (Bolarinwa, 2015). The questionnaires were also pilot-tested with a small group of 5-7 respondents to ensure dependability and address any concerns prior to the main data-gathering phase. An instrument’s reliability is related to its stability and consistency (Yunus & Ismail, 2024). In the context of questionnaire pretesting, revisions and further testing can enhance reliability. Prior to distributing the questionnaire, the researcher consulted experts, including PhD holders, who fully participated in the questionnaire distribution and all the study activities. Data analysis involves examining the collected data and making deductions and inferences. Primary data were collected through questionnaires administered via the Kobo Toolbox, downloaded in Excel format, and cleaned by verifying their completeness. The data were uploaded directly into SPSSV25.0 for qualitative and quantitative analyses. Descriptive statistics were used to organize, summarize, and present informative methods in the table as frequencies, percentages, means, and standard deviations to measure central tendency and dispersion. A multiple regression analysis was performed to investigate how employee training and motivation affect customer engagement in small and medium sized enterprises in BRMS. The regression equation used was Y=β+ β1X1+ β2X2 + ε, where Y represents the dependent variable, customer engagement (CL). The intercept β signifies the anticipated level of customer engagement when all independent variables (IVs) are absent. Coefficient β1 is linked to incentives (X1) and shows the change in customer engagement due to a one-unit change in this IV, while the other variables remain constant. Likewise, β2 is the coefficient for overtime payments (X2), demonstrating the impact of a one-unit change in this IV on customer engagement, with other factors held constant, and where ϵ denotes the error term. The researcher employed a model summary, ANOVA, and coefficient table analysis. In the model summary, the coefficient of determination (R2) reflects the proportion of variance in the dependent variable that can be explained by independent variables. The F-statistic evaluates whether the predictors explain a significant portion of the variance in Y, with a small p-value (typically p<0.05) indicating the model's significance. In the coefficient table, unstandardized coefficients and p-values were used to provide insights into the individual impact and significance of each predictor on the dependent variables. The model summary provides an overall assessment of model fit. The ANOVA table evaluates the overall significance of the regression, and the coefficient table provides detailed information on the impact and significance of each of the predictors.

This study examines the role of employee training and motivation in customer engagement among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the Banadir region of Mogadishu, Somalia. A descriptive quantitative approach was employed using structured questionnaires distributed to 172 employees of small businesses through a simple random sampling method. The results indicate that most respondents agreed that training improved key customer service skills, with agreement levels ranging from 58% to 72% (mean = 1.65, p < 0.05). It was also found that most respondents agreed with motivation-related statements, with agreement levels generally ranging from 55% to 63% (mean = 1.59, p < 0.05). Multiple regression analysis revealed that both employee training (B = 0.15, p < 0.05) and motivation (B = 0.049, p < 0.05) significantly contributed to predicting customer engagement. The model explains 9.7% of the variance in customer engagement (R2 = 0.097). The ANOVA results confirmed the reliability of the overall model in explaining the variations in customer engagement (F = 9.048, p < 0.05).  This study concludes that investments in employee training and motivational strategies are significantly associated with enhanced customer engagement in the context of Somali small and medium-sized enterprises. In practical Implications, the findings offer valuable insights for SME owners and managers in Somalia, highlighting that strategic investments in staff development and motivational programs are crucial for building strong customer relationships, improving service quality, and achieving sustainable competitive advantage.

In the contemporary competitive market, businesses, particularly smaller enterprises, recognize the significant influence of employees on customer satisfaction (CS) and engagement. Small businesses, especially in developing nations such as Somalia, face challenging conditions in which customer engagement is crucial for their survival and profitability. Employee training and motivation are widely recognized as essential human resource strategies that enhance service quality and foster customer engagement (Albrecht et al., 2015).Well-trained and motivated employees tend to demonstrate greater dedication, superior interpersonal skills, and increased efficiency, all of which are vital for delivering exceptional customer experiences and ensuring long-term engagement  (Katou, 2017). In China, customer engagement is a prominent subject in both academic and business discussions because of its impact on repeat purchases, client retention, and word-of-mouth marketing. In small business contexts with limited resources, customer engagement can determine the difference between business survival and failure (Rasool et al., 2020). According to this, research indicates that employees' skills, developed through ongoing training, and their motivation levels are closely linked to consumer perceptions of service quality, satisfaction, and engagement. When employees are motivated and well trained, they are more likely to consistently deliver excellent services, build trust, and maintain strong relationships with clients. In Africa, activities such as training and motivation are widely recognized as key drivers of customer engagement, particularly among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Studies show that well-trained and motivated staff enhance customer satisfaction, trust, and repeat purchasing behaviors, all of which are crucial for business survival in Africa's highly competitive markets. Moreover, employee engagement strategies have been associated with improved service quality and organizational performance in various African industries  (Deepalakshmi et al., 2024).  As African economies diversify, SMEs are encouraged to adopt human-centered management strategies to sustain their client engagement. This trend underscores the growing emphasis on human capital as a strategic asset for long-term business success.
In the Banadir Region of Mogadishu, particularly within the Bakara marketplace, small  and medium enterprises are prevalent in both the informal and formal sectors. These enterprises play a vital role in job creation and enhancing the local economy. Nevertheless, as competition intensifies and customer expectations increase, these businesses are compelled to improve their personnel management practices to enhance customer engagement. The unique socio-economic conditions in Somalia, particularly in the Banadir region, present significant challenges for this study. The country's economy is largely driven by the private sector, where small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) play a vital role in supporting livelihoods and promoting economic recovery, especially in the aftermath of conflict (Daka & Siad, 2022).  However, these businesses operate in a challenging environment characterized by weak institutional frameworks and a heavy reliance on informal business practices. A recent study by (Yusuf et al., 2024) on Islamic banks in Somalia emphasizes the importance of consumer trust, a factor that is also crucial for SMEs in the retail and service sectors. The study shows that reliability and strong customer relationships are key factors contributing to business success in an unstable environment. This aligns with the observation that Somali SMEs have traditionally developed with minimal formal human resource practices, making the formal adoption of training and motivational strategies a potential differentiator in building customer confidence and, ultimately, fostering customer engagement in Mogadishu’s competitive market. Although the role of employee training and motivation in building customer engagement has been widely studied in both global and African settings, there remains a significant lack of research focusing on Somalia’s specific situation. Small and medium-sized businesses (SMEs) in the Banadir Region and Mogadishu operate in a post-conflict environment characterized by weak and unstable institutions, limited formal structures, and intense market competition. These businesses play a vital role in the local economy; however, they often lack proper human resource management practices. The primary challenge is that, without relevant local data, the owners and managers of SMEs in Mogadishu do not have a clear understanding of how employee development and motivation influence customer engagement in the hospitality industry. Consequently, they tend to underinvest in these crucial areas, which can reduce their competitiveness and make it harder to retain customers and stay in business. Therefore, this study seeks to address this gap by examining how employee training and motivation enhance customer engagement among SMEs in the Banadir Region of Somalia. Thus; the specific objectives of this study is to investigate the role of employee training and motivation on customer engagement among small and medium sized enterprises in Banadir region, mogadishu, Somalia to maintain and enhance customer engagement across various markets.
2.1 Introduction
This chapter examines the current literature relevant to the study of the impact of employee motivation and training on customer engagement in small enterprises in the Banadir Region of Mogadishu, Somalia. It investigates the theories that support these notions and conducts empirical research on the impact of employee training and motivation on customer engagement in small business settings.
2.2 Theoretical Review
2.2.1 Resource-Based View (RBV) Theory
The Resource-Based View (RBV) theory suggests that an organization can achieve a competitive advantage by effectively utilizing internal resources that are valuable, rare, distinctive, and difficult to replace (Kaur, 2022). These internal resources include intangible factors, such as employee training and motivation, which help build essential competencies that improve overall performance within the organization. In the context of small businesses, it is crucial to recognize that well-trained and highly motivated employees are key to delivering high-quality customer service, thereby increasing customer satisfaction and engagement (Katou, 2017). According to RBV, human capital, particularly when it involves continuous development and motivation, can serve as a sustainable source of competitive advantage, especially in environments with limited financial resources such as Somalia. By investing in employee skills, small firms can differentiate themselves through the quality of services they provide, which can enhance customer engagement (Albrecht et al., 2015). In the RBV framework, employee training and motivation are recognized as strategic resources that contribute to customer interactions by improving service delivery and building trust, thereby creating long-lasting relationships between employees and customers.
2.2.2 Herzberg Two-Factor Theory
Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory of motivation identifies two types of factors that influence employee behavior: hygiene factors, such as salary and job security, and motivators, such as recognition, achievement, and responsibility (Thant & Chang, 2021). This study aligns with Herzberg’s theory, emphasizing that improving employee motivation can lead to better performance. Motivated employees are more likely to display positive attitudes toward customers, such as being friendly, attentive, and responsive, which are crucial for increasing customer satisfaction and involvement (Al-Dmour et al., 2021). (Katou, 2017) further highlights that well-motivated staff contribute to better service delivery, which, in turn, leads to greater consumer confidence and interaction. Herzberg’s Two-Factor Theory also shows that employee training and motivation are key drivers of employee satisfaction and performance (Asiamah et al., 2020). This connection can be understood through the Herzberg framework: training enhances employees' skills and confidence (motivators), while motivation maintains their commitment and enthusiasm for the organization, ultimately fostering better service behaviors that increase customer engagement and ensure long-term organizational success.

2.2.3 Social Exchange Theory (SET)
Social Exchange Theory (Blau, 1964) posits that relationships are built on the principle of reciprocal exchange, wherein individuals give and receive value. When employees receive training and encouragement, they are more likely to respond with positive attitudes and behaviors such as providing exceptional customer service. Customers who experience high-quality service are likely to feel valued and, therefore, develop loyalty to the organization. Social Exchange Theory highlights the link between human resource practices and customer outcomes, as well as the impact of employee treatment on customer interactions (Najam et al., 2020). From the customer’s perspective, SET explains how positive service experiences lead to increased customer engagement and retention. Customers who consistently receive excellent service from well-trained and motivated employees feel appreciated, which encourages them to make repeat purchases, engage in positive word-of-mouth, and refer the brand to others (Pérez, A., & Sánchez, 2021). Therefore, employee training and motivation play a significant role in fostering customer engagement according to the Social Exchange Theory, as they create mutual trust, satisfaction, and long-term relational exchanges between the organization and its customers.
2.3 Concept of Variables
2.3.1 Employee Training (IV1)
Employee training is an organizational strategic effort that endeavors to add skills, knowledge, and attitude to employees to improve their performance. Small businesses, especially those in volatile environments like Somalia, are the beneficiaries of continuous training to help employees cope with changing consumer needs, emerging technologies, and competition. Training enhances the confidence and capacities of employees, enabling them to pass correct information, handle complaints, and provide services tailored to the needs of the customer, all of which are important factors that determine customer engagement. Customer satisfaction is associated with training. On the one hand, (Albrecht et al., 2015) suggest that continuous training improves the quality of service and customer retention and trust. Moreover, qualified employees are better placed to identify customer needs, hence, enhancing relationships that facilitate engagement (Hemsley-Brown & Alnawas, 2016). It has been reported that in Africa, small- and middle-sized enterprises (SMEs) investing in employee training, as opposed to those that do not, have better performance particularly in industries that have a high number of client interactions coupled with high service quality (Deepalakshmi et al., 2024). The value of training in the study of the specific case of small businesses in Somalia is an issue that involves a considerable gap in knowledge because formal training structures are limited in the country (Yusuf et al., 2024).
2.3.2 Employee Motivation (IV2)
Employee motivation involves both intrinsic and extrinsic elements that enable employees to fulfill their roles in the workplace. Motivated employees are enthusiastic, committed, and proactive in customer service, which directly affects customer satisfaction and engagement (Aziri, 2019).The incentives that small businesses can use to motivate their employees include recognition, career growth, flexible working hours, and monetary rewards. Herzberg’s theory reveals that motivation is a major influence on job satisfaction and is linked to improved performance. In this study, (Rabbanee, Fazlul K.Ramaseshan, B.Vyravene, 2022) discovered that engaged employees were more motivated and, therefore, more engaged, which resulted in the enhancement of the client experience. Emotional commitment is also created through motivation, as seen in the interaction of staff members with clients, leading to a repeat of business and customer contact (Ibrahim et al., 2022). A study in Africa showed that motivation improves organizational performance by making employees provide the best customer services and create engagement through enjoyable experiences (Paais & Pattiruhu, 2020). Motivation is essential in service quality to retain customers and ensure that employee morale is maintained in places like Mogadishu, where economic realities might contribute to low employee morale.
2.3.3 Customer engagement (DV)
Customer engagement refers to the tendency of a customer to continuously buy from a company due to satisfaction, trust, and past experiences. In the case of small enterprises, engagement is of utmost importance because the cost of acquiring new customers is higher than that of retention. Customer engagement leads to steady income, an improved brand image, and a sustainable business in the long run (Zhao et al., 2021). Customers who are engaged will ensure that they get a repeat business besides the fact that they are part of word of mouth marketing which is essential especially in the Banadir market where word of mouth is greatly appreciated. This interaction is particularly important in Somalia, where companies must compete in an unstable market with a small number of customers. Customer engagement is promoted by trust, regular service quality, and positive relationships with motivated and well-trained employees (Saeed et al., 2022).
2.4 Employee training, Motivation and Customer engagement relationships.

The links between training, motivation, and customer engagement of employees have been widely discussed in the academic literature. Tacit knowledge has shown that human resource investment improves service quality and, hence, positively impacts consumer perceptions and involvement. Properly trained employees are prepared to provide excellent customer service, address any issues productively, and develop strong relationships with (Briggs et al., 2020). Politeness and empathy are good behaviors of motivated employees, which provide better customer satisfaction. The collaboration between employee training, employee engagement, and customer engagement is essential, as engaged and satisfied employees offer higher-quality services that would directly enhance customer satisfaction and retention. Companies that focus on the welfare of their employees often have higher consumer confidence and longer brand attachment (Srinivasan, 2024). Valued, motivated, and inspired employees are more likely to provide high-quality customer-driven services, leading to positive experiences among clients and, therefore, satisfaction and interaction. Involved employees are more receptive, friendly, and loyal to the company, a factor that has a direct impact on the perceptions of the customers of the business. Training, recognition, and support of employees by inspiring leaders make them more efficient in addressing problems (Paredes-Saavedra et al., 2024). The Resource-Based View emphasizes the importance of employee competencies and motivation to gain a competitive edge by interacting with customers (Kaur, 2022). Likewise, Herzberg’s theory argues that motivation drives employees to perform better than expected, leading to a good experience and interaction for the customer. The Social Exchange Theory states that reciprocal behaviors that benefit a customer are developed in organizations that invest in training and motivating their employees (Pérez, A., & Sánchez, 2021). In Somalia, the fact that human resource strategy is not formalized in small businesses means that an investor in training and motivation secures competitiveon advantage in improved relations with clients.
2.5 Empirical Review
Several studies have found a considerable relationship between employee-friendly policies and consumer engagement, as human resource strategies play an essential role in enhancing business performance. In this research, (Albrecht et al., 2015) discovered that organizations with extensive training programs and good motivation systems had significantly greater customer retention rates. According to their results, employee development improves the quality of services and, therefore, directly improves customer satisfaction and engagement. Similarly, (Endris & Kassegn, 2022) observed that SMEs that focus on employee growth and engagement have better interactions with customers and are likely to be more profitable. These businesses recognize that empowered employees are better placed to exceed expectations and bring about memorable experiences that will generate repeat business and instill customer engagement. As noted by (Deepalakshmi et al., 2024), to stand out in the market, SMEs in a highly competitive environment with limited resources tend to resort to human-based programs, inclusive communication, and training more frequently. These strategies enhance employee morale, which eventually affects the perception and interaction of customers with the company. The academic literature on this subject has been limited to the Somali setting. However, (Rabbanee, Fazlul K.Ramaseshan, B.Vyravene, 2022) suggested that employee satisfaction is critical to the perception of clients, especially in developing nations with emerging service industries. These articles underline the psychological correlation between internal employee morale and the perception of external clients.

ordered_content.text: 1. INTRODUCTION

In the contemporary competitive market, businesses, particularly smaller enterprises, recognize the significant influence of employees on customer satisfaction (CS) and engagement. Small businesses, especially in developing nations such as Somalia, face challenging conditions in which customer engagement is crucial for their survival and profitability. Employee training and motivation are widely recognized as essential human resource strategies that enhance service quality and foster customer engagement (Albrecht et al., 2015).Well-trained and motivated employees tend to demonstrate greater dedication, superior interpersonal skills, and increased efficiency, all of which are vital for delivering exceptional customer experiences and ensuring long-term engagement  (Katou, 2017). In China, customer engagement is a prominent subject in both academic and business discussions because of its impact on repeat purchases, client retention, and word-of-mouth marketing. In small business contexts with limited resources, customer engagement can determine the difference between business survival and failure (Rasool et al., 2020). According to this, research indicates that employees' skills, developed through ongoing training, and their motivation levels are closely linked to consumer perceptions of service quality, satisfaction, and engagement. When employees are motivated and well trained, they are more likely to consistently deliver excellent services, build trust, and maintain strong relationships with clients. In Africa, activities such as training and motivation are widely recognized as key drivers of customer engagement, particularly among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Studies show that well-trained and motivated staff enhance customer satisfaction, trust, and repeat purchasing behaviors, all of which are crucial for business survival in Africa's highly competitive markets. Moreover, employee engagement strategies have been associated with improved service quality and organizational performance in various African industries  (Deepalakshmi et al., 2024).  As African economies diversify, SMEs are encouraged to adopt human-centered management strategies to sustain their client engagement. This trend underscores the growing emphasis on human capital as a strategic asset for long-term business success.

ordered_content.text: In the Banadir Region of Mogadishu, particularly within the Bakara marketplace, small  and medium enterprises are prevalent in both the informal and formal sectors. These enterprises play a vital role in job creation and enhancing the local economy. Nevertheless, as competition intensifies and customer expectations increase, these businesses are compelled to improve their personnel management practices to enhance customer engagement. The unique socio-economic conditions in Somalia, particularly in the Banadir region, present significant challenges for this study. The country's economy is largely driven by the private sector, where small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) play a vital role in supporting livelihoods and promoting economic recovery, especially in the aftermath of conflict (Daka & Siad, 2022).  However, these businesses operate in a challenging environment characterized by weak institutional frameworks and a heavy reliance on informal business practices. A recent study by (Yusuf et al., 2024) on Islamic banks in Somalia emphasizes the importance of consumer trust, a factor that is also crucial for SMEs in the retail and service sectors. The study shows that reliability and strong customer relationships are key factors contributing to business success in an unstable environment. This aligns with the observation that Somali SMEs have traditionally developed with minimal formal human resource practices, making the formal adoption of training and motivational strategies a potential differentiator in building customer confidence and, ultimately, fostering customer engagement in Mogadishu’s competitive market. Although the role of employee training and motivation in building customer engagement has been widely studied in both global and African settings, there remains a significant lack of research focusing on Somalia’s specific situation. Small and medium-sized businesses (SMEs) in the Banadir Region and Mogadishu operate in a post-conflict environment characterized by weak and unstable institutions, limited formal structures, and intense market competition. These businesses play a vital role in the local economy; however, they often lack proper human resource management practices. The primary challenge is that, without relevant local data, the owners and managers of SMEs in Mogadishu do not have a clear understanding of how employee development and motivation influence customer engagement in the hospitality industry. Consequently, they tend to underinvest in these crucial areas, which can reduce their competitiveness and make it harder to retain customers and stay in business. Therefore, this study seeks to address this gap by examining how employee training and motivation enhance customer engagement among SMEs in the Banadir Region of Somalia. Thus; the specific objectives of this study is to investigate the role of employee training and motivation on customer engagement among small and medium sized enterprises in Banadir region, mogadishu, Somalia to maintain and enhance customer engagement across various markets.

It investigates the theories that support these notions and conducts empirical research on the impact of employee training and motivation on customer engagement in small business settings.

2.2.1 Resource-Based View (RBV) Theory

The Resource-Based View (RBV) theory suggests that an organization can achieve a competitive advantage by effectively utilizing internal resources that are valuable, rare, distinctive, and difficult to replace (Kaur, 2022). These internal resources include intangible factors, such as employee training and motivation, which help build essential competencies that improve overall performance within the organization. In the context of small businesses, it is crucial to recognize that well-trained and highly motivated employees are key to delivering high-quality customer service, thereby increasing customer satisfaction and engagement (Katou, 2017). According to RBV, human capital, particularly when it involves continuous development and motivation, can serve as a sustainable source of competitive advantage, especially in environments with limited financial resources such as Somalia. By investing in employee skills, small firms can differentiate themselves through the quality of services they provide, which can enhance customer engagement (Albrecht et al., 2015). In the RBV framework, employee training and motivation are recognized as strategic resources that contribute to customer interactions by improving service delivery and building trust, thereby creating long-lasting relationships between employees and customers.

ordered_content.text: 2.2.2 Herzberg Two-Factor Theory

Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory of motivation identifies two types of factors that influence employee behavior: hygiene factors, such as salary and job security, and motivators, such as recognition, achievement, and responsibility (Thant & Chang, 2021). This study aligns with Herzberg’s theory, emphasizing that improving employee motivation can lead to better performance. Motivated employees are more likely to display positive attitudes toward customers, such as being friendly, attentive, and responsive, which are crucial for increasing customer satisfaction and involvement (Al-Dmour et al., 2021). (Katou, 2017) further highlights that well-motivated staff contribute to better service delivery, which, in turn, leads to greater consumer confidence and interaction. Herzberg’s Two-Factor Theory also shows that employee training and motivation are key drivers of employee satisfaction and performance (Asiamah et al., 2020). This connection can be understood through the Herzberg framework: training enhances employees' skills and confidence (motivators), while motivation maintains their commitment and enthusiasm for the organization, ultimately fostering better service behaviors that increase customer engagement and ensure long-term organizational success.

ordered_content.text: 2.2.3 Social Exchange Theory (SET)

Social Exchange Theory (Blau, 1964) posits that relationships are built on the principle of reciprocal exchange, wherein individuals give and receive value. When employees receive training and encouragement, they are more likely to respond with positive attitudes and behaviors such as providing exceptional customer service. Customers who experience high-quality service are likely to feel valued and, therefore, develop loyalty to the organization. Social Exchange Theory highlights the link between human resource practices and customer outcomes, as well as the impact of employee treatment on customer interactions (Najam et al., 2020). From the customer’s perspective, SET explains how positive service experiences lead to increased customer engagement and retention. Customers who consistently receive excellent service from well-trained and motivated employees feel appreciated, which encourages them to make repeat purchases, engage in positive word-of-mouth, and refer the brand to others (Pérez, A., & Sánchez, 2021). Therefore, employee training and motivation play a significant role in fostering customer engagement according to the Social Exchange Theory, as they create mutual trust, satisfaction, and long-term relational exchanges between the organization and its customers.

ordered_content.text: 2.3 Concept of Variables
2.3.1 Employee Training (IV1)

Employee training is an organizational strategic effort that endeavors to add skills, knowledge, and attitude to employees to improve their performance. Small businesses, especially those in volatile environments like Somalia, are the beneficiaries of continuous training to help employees cope with changing consumer needs, emerging technologies, and competition. Training enhances the confidence and capacities of employees, enabling them to pass correct information, handle complaints, and provide services tailored to the needs of the customer, all of which are important factors that determine customer engagement. Customer satisfaction is associated with training. On the one hand, (Albrecht et al., 2015) suggest that continuous training improves the quality of service and customer retention and trust. Moreover, qualified employees are better placed to identify customer needs, hence, enhancing relationships that facilitate engagement (Hemsley-Brown & Alnawas, 2016). It has been reported that in Africa, small- and middle-sized enterprises (SMEs) investing in employee training, as opposed to those that do not, have better performance particularly in industries that have a high number of client interactions coupled with high service quality (Deepalakshmi et al., 2024). The value of training in the study of the specific case of small businesses in Somalia is an issue that involves a considerable gap in knowledge because formal training structures are limited in the country (Yusuf et al., 2024).

ordered_content.text: 2.3.2 Employee Motivation (IV2)

Employee motivation involves both intrinsic and extrinsic elements that enable employees to fulfill their roles in the workplace. Motivated employees are enthusiastic, committed, and proactive in customer service, which directly affects customer satisfaction and engagement (Aziri, 2019).The incentives that small businesses can use to motivate their employees include recognition, career growth, flexible working hours, and monetary rewards. Herzberg’s theory reveals that motivation is a major influence on job satisfaction and is linked to improved performance. In this study, (Rabbanee, Fazlul K.Ramaseshan, B.Vyravene, 2022) discovered that engaged employees were more motivated and, therefore, more engaged, which resulted in the enhancement of the client experience. Emotional commitment is also created through motivation, as seen in the interaction of staff members with clients, leading to a repeat of business and customer contact (Ibrahim et al., 2022). A study in Africa showed that motivation improves organizational performance by making employees provide the best customer services and create engagement through enjoyable experiences (Paais & Pattiruhu, 2020). Motivation is essential in service quality to retain customers and ensure that employee morale is maintained in places like Mogadishu, where economic realities might contribute to low employee morale.

ordered_content.text: 2.3.3 Customer engagement (DV)

Customer engagement refers to the tendency of a customer to continuously buy from a company due to satisfaction, trust, and past experiences. In the case of small enterprises, engagement is of utmost importance because the cost of acquiring new customers is higher than that of retention. Customer engagement leads to steady income, an improved brand image, and a sustainable business in the long run (Zhao et al., 2021). Customers who are engaged will ensure that they get a repeat business besides the fact that they are part of word of mouth marketing which is essential especially in the Banadir market where word of mouth is greatly appreciated. This interaction is particularly important in Somalia, where companies must compete in an unstable market with a small number of customers. Customer engagement is promoted by trust, regular service quality, and positive relationships with motivated and well-trained employees (Saeed et al., 2022).

Tacit knowledge has shown that human resource investment improves service quality and, hence, positively impacts consumer perceptions and involvement. Properly trained employees are prepared to provide excellent customer service, address any issues productively, and develop strong relationships with (Briggs et al., 2020). Politeness and empathy are good behaviors of motivated employees, which provide better customer satisfaction. The collaboration between employee training, employee engagement, and customer engagement is essential, as engaged and satisfied employees offer higher-quality services that would directly enhance customer satisfaction and retention. Companies that focus on the welfare of their employees often have higher consumer confidence and longer brand attachment (Srinivasan, 2024). Valued, motivated, and inspired employees are more likely to provide high-quality customer-driven services, leading to positive experiences among clients and, therefore, satisfaction and interaction. Involved employees are more receptive, friendly, and loyal to the company, a factor that has a direct impact on the perceptions of the customers of the business. Training, recognition, and support of employees by inspiring leaders make them more efficient in addressing problems (Paredes-Saavedra et al., 2024). The Resource-Based View emphasizes the importance of employee competencies and motivation to gain a competitive edge by interacting with customers (Kaur, 2022). Likewise, Herzberg’s theory argues that motivation drives employees to perform better than expected, leading to a good experience and interaction for the customer. The Social Exchange Theory states that reciprocal behaviors that benefit a customer are developed in organizations that invest in training and motivating their employees (Pérez, A., & Sánchez, 2021). In Somalia, the fact that human resource strategy is not formalized in small businesses means that an investor in training and motivation secures competitiveon advantage in improved relations with clients.

ordered_content.text: 2.5 Empirical Review

Several studies have found a considerable relationship between employee-friendly policies and consumer engagement, as human resource strategies play an essential role in enhancing business performance. In this research, (Albrecht et al., 2015) discovered that organizations with extensive training programs and good motivation systems had significantly greater customer retention rates. According to their results, employee development improves the quality of services and, therefore, directly improves customer satisfaction and engagement. Similarly, (Endris & Kassegn, 2022) observed that SMEs that focus on employee growth and engagement have better interactions with customers and are likely to be more profitable. These businesses recognize that empowered employees are better placed to exceed expectations and bring about memorable experiences that will generate repeat business and instill customer engagement. As noted by (Deepalakshmi et al., 2024), to stand out in the market, SMEs in a highly competitive environment with limited resources tend to resort to human-based programs, inclusive communication, and training more frequently. These strategies enhance employee morale, which eventually affects the perception and interaction of customers with the company. The academic literature on this subject has been limited to the Somali setting. However, (Rabbanee, Fazlul K.Ramaseshan, B.Vyravene, 2022) suggested that employee satisfaction is critical to the perception of clients, especially in developing nations with emerging service industries. These articles underline the psychological correlation between internal employee morale and the perception of external clients.

3. MATERIAL AND METHODS

This section outlines the research framework, sampling techniques and data analysis procedures. A descriptive research design with a quantitative focus was selected as optimal for examining the relationship between employee training, motivation, and customer engagement. This approach enabled orderly data collection and analysis, which was aligned with the study objectives. Employing a quantitative method and multiple regression analysis is considered appropriate for the research goals because it enhances the simplicity, generalizability, clarity, and statistical reliability. The analysis utilized frequencies, tables, percentages, and regression analyses to address the research question: "What effect do employee training and motivation have on customer engagement among small and medium enterprises in Mogadishu, Somalia?" Structured questionnaires were developed based on a comprehensive literature review, employing Likert scales (2= Agree,1 = Disagree) via the Kobo Toolbox to collect data from employees of small and medium-sized organizations. This platform ensures efficiency, reduces manual errors, and facilitates smooth data cleaning and export to statistical software programs. Data collection will be conducted from November 2024 to January 2025. The questionnaires were personally distributed with the assistance of leaders, managers and supervisors to gather data from staff working in small and medium sized enterprises in Mogadishu and Somalia. The researchers ensured that the distribution of the questionnaires did not interfere with the respondents' official work schedules and obtained special permission from the company leaders. The data were analyzed after cleaning and verifying the questionnaires’ completeness. The researchers utilized a simple random sampling technique, a type of probability sampling, to ensure that each individual had an equal chance of being selected, thereby accurately representing the target population (Tabiu, 2017). This method aligns with the objective of obtaining representative samples while maintaining methodological rigor. The validity of the findings was enhanced by ensuring that each participant had an equal probability of being selected. The researchers identified 301 respondents and distributed 172 questionnaires to employees of small- and medium-sized enterprises in Mogadishu, Somalia. The participants were staff members of small- and medium-sized enterprises, excluding non-staff members and those employed in non-business organizations. Slovin’s formula was employed to determine the sample size with a maximum allowable error of 5%, where n= 31/1+301 (0.05)2=172, where n represents the sample size, N is the population, and a is the acceptable error. This formula was selected because it allows sampling of the population with the desired precision. The sample size ensured representativeness with a 95% confidence level, providing a reliable estimate of population characteristics consistent with the research's quantitative objectives.  To ensure the accuracy of the data, the questionnaires were examined by specialists with an understanding of staff training, motivation, and customer engagement among SME's in the Banadir region of Mogadishu, Somalia, ensuring that they included all important parts of the study. This means that it communicates accurate data that are compatible with respondents’ information and expectations. The quantity of built-in measurement errors determines the validity of the research instrument (Bolarinwa, 2015). The questionnaires were also pilot-tested with a small group of 5-7 respondents to ensure dependability and address any concerns prior to the main data-gathering phase. An instrument’s reliability is related to its stability and consistency (Yunus & Ismail, 2024). In the context of questionnaire pretesting, revisions and further testing can enhance reliability. Prior to distributing the questionnaire, the researcher consulted experts, including PhD holders, who fully participated in the questionnaire distribution and all the study activities. Data analysis involves examining the collected data and making deductions and inferences. Primary data were collected through questionnaires administered via the Kobo Toolbox, downloaded in Excel format, and cleaned by verifying their completeness. The data were uploaded directly into SPSSV25.0 for qualitative and quantitative analyses. Descriptive statistics were used to organize, summarize, and present informative methods in the table as frequencies, percentages, means, and standard deviations to measure central tendency and dispersion. A multiple regression analysis was performed to investigate how employee training and motivation affect customer engagement in small and medium sized enterprises in BRMS. The regression equation used was Y=β+ β1X1+ β2X2 + ε, where Y represents the dependent variable, customer engagement (CL). The intercept β signifies the anticipated level of customer engagement when all independent variables (IVs) are absent. Coefficient β1 is linked to incentives (X1) and shows the change in customer engagement due to a one-unit change in this IV, while the other variables remain constant. Likewise, β2 is the coefficient for overtime payments (X2), demonstrating the impact of a one-unit change in this IV on customer engagement, with other factors held constant, and where ϵ denotes the error term. The researcher employed a model summary, ANOVA, and coefficient table analysis. In the model summary, the coefficient of determination (R2) reflects the proportion of variance in the dependent variable that can be explained by independent variables. The F-statistic evaluates whether the predictors explain a significant portion of the variance in Y, with a small p-value (typically p<0.05) indicating the model's significance. In the coefficient table, unstandardized coefficients and p-values were used to provide insights into the individual impact and significance of each predictor on the dependent variables. The model summary provides an overall assessment of model fit. The ANOVA table evaluates the overall significance of the regression, and the coefficient table provides detailed information on the impact and significance of each of the predictors.

ordered_content.text: 5. DISCUSSION OF FINDINGS

This study investigates the influence of employee training and motivation on customer engagement in small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the Banadir region of Mogadishu, Somalia. The descriptive findings from Objective One revealed that a substantial proportion of participants (72%) agreed that trained employees effectively and accurately responded to customer inquiries, as evidenced by a high mean score of 1.72, indicating proficient customer service quality. However, aspects related to encouraging positive customer feedback and relationship building exhibited lower agreement levels (58%), suggesting potential areas for improvement in customer connections and emotional engagement in the hospitality industry. Regarding Objective Two, the analysis of employee motivation demonstrated that most employees acknowledged the significance of fostering positive customer interactions (63%) and exceeding customer expectations (61%), supporting the premise that motivated employees enhance the customer experience. Nevertheless, the perception that motivation influences employee engagement had a lower mean (1.55) and higher disagreement (45%), indicating that while motivation enhances performance, its impact on engagement may require additional organizational support or incentives to be fully realized. Regression analysis identified a statistically significant relationship between employee training, motivation, and customer engagement in SMEs in the Banadir Region. Both independent variables positively affected customer engagement, with employee training exerting a slightly greater influence. The model exhibited moderate explanatory power, suggesting that while these factors are significant, other elements may contribute to customer engagement. The ANOVA results validated the overall model, confirming that the predictors effectively accounted for variations in the dependent variable. These findings highlight the importance of investing in employee development and motivational strategies to strengthen customer relationships. Consequently, SMEs in the region should prioritize skill development, motivational strategies, and broader customer-centric policies to enhance sustainable engagement.

ordered_content.text: 6. CONCLUSION

This study elucidates the significant influence of employee training and motivation on enhancing customer engagement among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the Banadir Region of Mogadishu, Somalia. The findings revealed that well-trained employees deliver services with greater speed and accuracy, while motivated personnel cultivate positive customer interactions, both of which contribute to increased customer satisfaction (CS). Regression analysis confirmed that both training and motivation were significant predictors of engagement, with training having a slightly stronger effect. These findings highlight the necessity of continuous skill enhancement and motivation through incentives to maintain customer relationships. The relatively low R² value suggests that although these factors are crucial, other elements also contribute to fostering greater engagement. This study addresses the gap in the literature on Somali SMEs by providing empirical evidence of the relationship between human resource practices and customer outcomes. In conclusion, strategic investment in human capital is essential for achieving competitive advantage and sustainable growth.

Based on the outcomes of the study, The researchers recommended that small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the Banadir Region should implement the organized and ongoing employee training programs aimed to improve customer service competencies, communication, and problem-solving skills. Managers should also adopt motivation systems like recognition programs, performance based reward and career growth to maintain the morale and productivity of employees. Business associations and policymakers ought to work together to offer capacity-building programs that can enable the SMEs to institutionalize the human resource development practices. With a more robust employee competencies combined with motivation, organizations can achieve elevated customer participation, satisfaction, and customer loyalty thus playing a role in achieving sustainable business growth in the competitive market situations in Somalia.

first_page_metadata.abstract:
This study examines the role of employee training and motivation in customer engagement among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the Banadir region of Mogadishu, Somalia. A descriptive quantitative approach was employed using structured questionnaires distributed to 172 employees of small businesses through a simple random sampling method. The results indicate that most respondents agreed that training improved key customer service skills, with agreement levels ranging from 58% to 72% (mean = 1.65, p < 0.05). It was also found that most respondents agreed with motivation-related statements, with agreement levels generally ranging from 55% to 63% (mean = 1.59, p < 0.05). Multiple regression analysis revealed that both employee training (B = 0.15, p < 0.05) and motivation (B = 0.049, p < 0.05) significantly contributed to predicting customer engagement. The model explains 9.7% of the variance in customer engagement (R2 = 0.097). The ANOVA results confirmed the reliability of the overall model in explaining the variations in customer engagement (F = 9.048, p < 0.05).  This study concludes that investments in employee training and motivational strategies are significantly associated with enhanced customer engagement in the context of Somali small and medium-sized enterprises. In practical Implications, the findings offer valuable insights for SME owners and managers in Somalia, highlighting that strategic investments in staff development and motivational programs are crucial for building strong customer relationships, improving service quality, and achieving sustainable competitive advantage.
